planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or hanging basket of chunky, well-drained fern or aroid mix in bright shade to filtered light; Phymatosorus diversifolius spreads from a thick, fuzzy, creeping rhizome that roots along the soil surface and is easily divided for propagation. Outdoors it is hardy only in frost-free zones but makes an excellent houseplant or shaded patio container elsewhere.

directions: Plant in bright, indirect light or deep shade in a loose, fast-draining potting mix, and keep the thick, hairy rhizome partly exposed on the soil surface rather than buried, since it is prone to rot if covered too deeply. Phymatosorus diversifolius (kangaroo fern, kangaroo paw fern) is a creeping epiphytic or terrestrial fern native to Australia and New Zealand, grown for its glossy, deeply lobed, leathery fronds that emerge singly along a wandering, scaly rhizome rather than forming a central crown. It tolerates lower humidity and more neglect than many tropical ferns, making it a popular low-maintenance houseplant or hanging-basket subject, and spreads readily in a shaded, frost-free garden bed. Water when the top inch of soil dries and avoid letting the rhizome sit in standing water.

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or shallow pot of moist, peaty, well-drained mix in bright shade with high humidity; Asplenium daucifolium produces tiny plantlets along its finely divided, carrot-leaf-like fronds that root readily when they touch moist soil, giving the plant its common name and making propagation effortless.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered shade with consistently moist (not waterlogged) peaty soil and elevated humidity; Asplenium daucifolium, the mother fern, is a Madagascar-native epiphytic/terrestrial species prized for its finely dissected, ferny, carrot-leaf-textured fronds, a texture distinct from the broad undivided fronds of its better-known relative Asplenium nidus. Small plantlets form along the frond surface and drop off to root wherever they contact moist media, so the plant naturalizes readily in a shaded, humid greenhouse bench or terrarium and is often grown in a hanging basket to display the pendent, plantlet-studded fronds. Keep out of direct sun, which scorches the delicate foliage, and protect from temperatures below 50°F.
sources: Dave's Garden PlantFiles — Asplenium daucifolium (Mother Fern)
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Asplenium bulbiferum / daucifolium group

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Dryopteris crassirhizoma forms a substantial, upright, shuttlecock-shaped clump from a thick, scaly rhizome and is one of the larger and more statuesque East Asian wood ferns in cultivation. Native to the forests of Japan, Korea, northern China, and the Russian Far East, it is valued in gardens for its bold, dark-green, semi-evergreen fronds and in traditional East Asian medicine (as 'guan zhong') for its rhizome, though the plant is grown ornamentally here strictly as a handsome woodland-garden specimen. It combines well with hostas and other shade perennials and is slow to establish but long-lived once settled.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery — Dryopteris crassirhizoma

planting.note: Grow in a pot or shaded bed of moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright shade; 'Parkeri' is a broader-leaved, more robust selection of Cretan brake fern than the species type, distinguished from the already-common variegated 'Albolineata' by its solid green, un-striped fronds with wider, more overlapping pinnae.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or partial shade in evenly moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; 'Parkeri' is a long-cultivated, solid-green cultivar of Pteris cretica selected for its broader, more densely overlapping pinnae and more robust, compact habit compared with the species type. Unlike the silver-striped 'Albolineata' or the crested 'Wilsonii' already common in cultivation, 'Parkeri' is grown purely for its clean, glossy, undivided-looking green foliage, making it a reliable, easy-care houseplant or shaded container fern. It tolerates lower humidity than many tropical ferns and is a long-standing favorite of Victorian-era fernery collections still grown today.
sources: The Evergreen Nursery — Pteris cretica 'Parkeri'

planting.note: Grow in a large pot or shaded bed of rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in warm, humid, filtered shade; Adiantum trapeziforme is among the largest maidenhair ferns in cultivation, with broad, diamond-shaped pinnae on arching fronds, and needs more warmth and humidity than hardy Adiantum species already in the dataset.

directions: Grow in warm, humid, filtered shade in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, sheltered from drying wind and direct sun. Adiantum trapeziforme, the giant or diamond maidenhair fern, is a large tropical American species that produces broad, wedge-shaped (trapezoid) pinnae on long, gracefully arching black stipes, giving it a bolder and more dramatic presence than the smaller hardy maidenhairs. It requires consistently high humidity and will brown at the leaf edges in dry indoor air, so it is best suited to a greenhouse, terrarium, or shaded, humid patio in frost-free climates. Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and to maintain vigor.
sources: Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Garden Explorer: Adiantum trapeziforme

planting.note: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded bed of moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; 'Furcans' is a crested, forked-frond-tip sword fern selection distinct from the already-cataloged Boston fern cultivars of Nephrolepis exaltata, with narrower, more finely divided, antler-like pinnae tips.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, and water whenever the top inch of soil dries. Nephrolepis falcata 'Furcans' is a crested sword-fern cultivar prized for its narrow, deeply cut pinnae that repeatedly fork at the tips into fine, fishtail- or antler-like points, giving the fronds a much lacier, more textured appearance than the broad, undivided pinnae of common Boston fern cultivars. It forms a dense, arching, fountain-like clump well suited to a hanging basket on a shaded porch or as a shade-garden accent in frost-free climates, and like other Nephrolepis it spreads by wiry surface runners that can be divided to propagate new plants.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 10-12; Aglaonema modestum is the original plain-green 'Chinese evergreen' species from which many of the patterned, variegated cultivars already in the dataset were later selected and bred. It is one of the most shade- and low-light-tolerant Aglaonema species, surviving conditions that would stress the showier patterned hybrids.

directions: Grow in low to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich potting soil, watering when the top inch of soil dries; Aglaonema modestum tolerates deeper shade and lower light than almost any other Aglaonema in cultivation, which made it an early, enduring staple of low-light interior plantscaping long before the patterned cultivars became popular. The foliage is a solid, glossy, unpatterned deep green, lance-shaped to elliptical, borne on a clumping, slow-spreading stem base. It is native to woodland understory from southeastern China and Indo-China south into the Philippines. Because it is unpatterned, it is grown more for its toughness and reliability in difficult low-light interiors than for ornamental drama, and it combines well as a textural foil for variegated foliage plants. All parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online: Aglaonema modestum

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container in zone 10-12; Aglaonema simplex is a slender, cane-forming woodland species from Southeast Asia distinct from the broader-leaved commutatum/costatum/pictum cultivar groups already in the dataset, with both plain-green and lightly variegated forms in cultivation.

directions: Grow in low to bright indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping the soil lightly moist but never soggy. Aglaonema simplex is a slender, upright, cane-like species native to the understory of lowland rainforests from Indochina through Malaysia to the Philippines, where it grows in deep shade on the forest floor. Its narrow, lance-shaped leaves are typically a glossy mid- to dark-green, sometimes with faint silvery mottling along the midrib in wild-collected forms, giving it a more delicate, reed-like silhouette than the broader, bushier cultivated Aglaonema hybrids. It is a true deep-shade understory aroid and tolerates lower light levels than most of the showier patterned cultivars. All parts are toxic if ingested.
sources: International Aroid Society (aroid.org) — Aglaonema simplex species profile

planting.note: Grow in full to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or chunky aroid mix; Syngonium rayii spreads as a creeping groundcover via long, leafless runners ('flagella') rather than climbing vigorously like most cultivated Syngonium podophyllum selections already in the dataset.

directions: Grow in deep to partial shade in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or a chunky aroid mix; Syngonium rayii is a Central American (Costa Rica and Panama) rainforest-floor aroid grown for its dark, almost blackish-green, velvety, arrowhead-shaped leaves, which often show a fine silvery midrib stripe in juvenile growth that fades as the leaf matures. Rather than climbing a support the way most cultivated Syngonium podophyllum forms do, it spreads low across the ground via long, leafless, rooting runners called flagella, making it a distinctive shade groundcover or trailing container plant. It prefers warmth, high humidity, and protection from direct sun, which will scorch the velvety leaf surface. CAUTION: like other Syngonium, all parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic to pets and people if ingested.
sources: International Aroid Society — Syngonium rayii species notes

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, humid patio container in zone 10-12; Ctenanthe compressa is a taller, solid fresh-green-leaved species distinct from the patterned burle-marxii, oppenheimiana, and setosa cultivars already in the dataset, and needs higher humidity than most houseplants to prevent leaf curl.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light or partial shade, never direct sun, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil with consistently high humidity. Ctenanthe compressa is a Brazilian rainforest-understory relative of the prayer-plant family (Marantaceae) that forms an upright clump of long, oblong, glossy fresh-green leaves on slender canes, reaching considerably taller than the lower, mounding burle-marxii and setosa forms already common in cultivation. Like other Ctenanthe it exhibits nyctinastic leaf movement, raising its leaves toward vertical at night. It is more sensitive to low humidity than many houseplants and will develop curled, crisping leaf margins in dry indoor air, so it benefits from a pebble tray, humidifier, or greenhouse-like setting. Keep away from cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F.
